extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists, humor writers, editors, and readers interested in the psychology and craft of cartoon humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and psychological principles for creating or evaluating cartoons (especially single-panel and editorial cartoons) that reliably produce humor, emotional effects, or cross-cultural resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-resolution (surprise + resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter often arises when a cartoon creates a gap between expectation and outcome (surprise) that then resolves into something that makes sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly referenced as the 'incongruity-resolution theory'. Effective jokes generate an expectation, then flip or violate it, and provide a quick cognitive resolution so the reader experiences the 'aha' that produces laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity / visual simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke requires quick visual processing; cluttered or confusing images can block the joke entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep imagery simple and readable so the brain can process the setup in under ~100 ms. Anti-pattern: overly busy panels that slow comprehension and prevent the punchline from landing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing in still images (visual rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even single-panel cartoons rely on timing—how the eye moves through the image creates a rhythm that sets up and delivers the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange elements, facial expressions, and text to guide the reader's gaze through a setup and to a punchline moment. Think in terms of sequencing and visual pacing despite the image being static.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guided eye movement / delayed reveal
rubrics_metrics.description: Smart cartoonists deliberately guide the viewer's eye to create delayed reveals—building expectation and then offering a late detail that flips the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use composition, placement of details, and text location to control reading order. Delayed reveal is an intentional misdirection technique: withhold the surprising element until the eye has set up the wrong interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption brevity / avoid over-explaining
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining the joke in the caption kills the surprise and reduces humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep captions minimal and let the image do the heavy lifting. Anti-pattern: captions that restate or clarify the punchline rather than enhancing the incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the cartoon's tone is unclear, readers may be uncertain whether they should laugh, making the joke ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal whether the piece is satirical, sarcastic, unsettling, or playful through visual cues and wording. Ambiguous tone reduces emotional payoff and can confuse or alienate audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sarcasm and satire mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sarcastic/satirical cartoons work by tapping psychological triggers: making the reader feel clever for understanding subtext, offering relief from tension, and creating social bonding among those 'in the know.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume an audience that can read subtext; use sparing, sharp subversion rather than blunt statements. Editorial cartoons benefit from expecting readers to grasp cultural subtext; anti-pattern: heavy-handed satire that leaves no subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural universality vs local references
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual humor based on facial expressions, physical comedy, or universal absurdities tends to travel across cultures; wordplay or culturally specific references may not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For international reach, emphasize universally shared human experiences and nonverbal cues. Beware that teasing or norms in one culture may be disrespectful or confusing in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of facial expressions and visual shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Facial expressions and simple visual cues are fast signals the brain reads first and can carry much of the joke's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage exaggerated but readable expressions and easily decoded symbols to communicate setup or punchline quickly. These cues are often more effective than verbose explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance accessibility and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful cartoons are accessible enough for quick comprehension yet surprising enough to generate genuine laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for broad-enough setup that readers can understand quickly, then introduce a twist that is unexpected but coherent. Avoid making jokes so obscure they require extra explanation, or so obvious they lack payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic use of 'cartoon jump scares'
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cartoons employ abrupt, unsettling surprise (jump scares) to provoke reactions that may include laughter, shock, or mild discomfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this disruptive technique sparingly; its strength comes from rarity. It's not a traditional punchline-driven laugh but a deliberate expectation disruption to provoke a visceral response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional and physiological benefits (stress relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humorous cartoons can produce measurable psychological effects—releasing dopamine and endorphins and reducing cortisol—providing quick emotional resets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design cartoons to be short, easily consumed moments that can lift mood or reduce stress (useful in workplace or healthcare settings). This is a feature to consider when choosing tone and complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding tone/content misfires across cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: What is gentle teasing in one culture may be serious disrespect in another; tone and content choices affect cross-cultural reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for international audiences, prefer shared experiences and nonverbal humor; test culturally specific jokes for possible misinterpretation or offense.
